extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical standards for public relations counsel on how to understand, reach, and influence public opinion using media, crowd psychology, timing, and established communication channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist the established point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: The moulder of public opinion must enlist the established point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with, not simply against, prevailing opinions; realize newspapers and other forces must appeal to the public that buys them. Example: press must balance carrying both pleasant and unpleasant news while recognizing possibilities for selective action to keep up community morale (New York Tribune ad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain editorial courage and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to 'brave the public' and consistently stand for the policies of your organization even when the public is hostile or cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two Baltimore Suns are cited as exemplars that refused to yield to pressure; such bravery can gradually change or at least retain integrity with sections of the public. Counsel should expect give-and-take between institution and public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the 'mirrors of the public mind' (media and platforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the press, motion pictures, lecture platforms, and other media to see what standards they have and which groups they reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these media as diagnostic tools to reveal group standards and constituencies; this is necessary to determine where and how to present a point of view effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover the stimuli to which public opinion responds
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what stimuli the public most readily responds to before attempting to modify viewpoints or policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond noting interaction between institutions and public, the counsel must 'go deeper' and identify the concrete stimuli and triggers for receptive responses in the target groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground work in individual and group psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental study of group and individual psychology is required to determine how readily individuals or groups will accept modifications of viewpoints or policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand motivations, stereotypes, herd instincts, and other psychological mechanisms; these form the groundwork for selecting methods and anticipating resistance or acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and respect stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that psychological 'stereotypes' (shorthand images like 'capitalist' or 'boy scout') largely determine what facts people will see and how they will interpret them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereotypes are influential and hard to change; counsel must inquire into their origins and why they are difficult to affect, and tailor messaging that fits or carefully reshapes these mental patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize crowd-mind as a pervasive state, not just physical crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'crowd' is a state of mind that can occur even when people are solitary; readers, listeners, movie-goers often react as parts of a crowd-mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communications assuming individual recipients may process messages with crowd-psychology effects (boosting, identification, simplified responses). Examples: book readers, solitary radio listeners, and movie audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage herd homogeneity and the desire for identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Herd homogeneity makes groups more likely to accept suggestions coming from the herd; people fear physical and mental solitude and seek identification with a class or herd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularize ideas by securing herd support and signaling group membership; use perceived majority or class cues to make messages acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit the herd's susceptibility to leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals in herds are remarkably susceptible to leadership; leaders who satisfy impulses (not always rational analysis) can mobilize herd action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and use credible leaders or proxies to champion messages; be aware leadership need not withstand rigorous analysis if it satisfies group impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and respect the group's resistance to change
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups resist fundamental change because members have sacrificed individual freedom to remain within the group and develop 'logic-proof' compartments that dismiss contrary standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect entrenched rationalizations and reluctance; plan incremental or sympathetic approaches and avoid frontal assaults that threaten group identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match cause to group reaction and tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause represented must have some group reaction and tradition in common with the public being targeted before they can react sympathetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze traditions, historical affinities and shared fundamentals; without baseline compatibility, persuasion efforts will likely fail or provoke backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use timing and salience (what else happened that day)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prominence a paper or medium gives to an occurrence depends on competing events and what else happened that day; timing affects whether semi-news or important news is featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose moments when 'real news' is scarce or when competing events won't drown the message; understand editorial winnowing and plan for salience and headline competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor content to the medium's constituency and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and other media select and emphasize items to fit their scheme and constituency—there are conventions rather than objective standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt tone, content, and placement to the traditions and expected tastes of each medium's audience (e.g., New York Sun vs. World vs. Evening Post).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reach the public only through established communication mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can be reached only through established mediums of communication; in a heterogeneous modern society an expert is needed to reach diverse groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which established channels (print, film, radio, lectures, etc.) effectively reach target subgroups; direct appeals via unknown or novel channels will be ineffective at national scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work within limits—public opinion is not fully manufacturable
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must continually realize there are limitations: public opinion is not manufactured ex nihilo, nor does it wholly determine institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overclaiming responsibility for creating opinion; instead, amplify, redirect, or capitalize on existing tendencies and be realistic about achievable change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome the mind's internal censorship (logic-proof compartments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual minds act as the world's most efficient censor—'logic-proof' compartments and absolutism are obstacles to perception and acceptance of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages to bypass or gradually alter internal censorship by using trusted messengers, aligning with group cues, and reducing cognitive dissonance rather than confronting it directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve accuracy, fairness, and credibility to secure cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy and fairness are essential to secure cooperation of other media and to present facts without exaggeration (example: The World’s Klan series prompted other papers to join because they trusted the World’s accuracy and fairness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build reputational capital; public-service framing, truthful reporting, and consistent fairness attract collaboration and reduce charges of sensationalism or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the duty to community morale in times of stress
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions (e.g., newspapers) have a hard and fast duty in keeping up the morale of the community during stress, which influences editorial selection and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising clients, factor in communal morale and the ethical/social consequences of messaging; sometimes selective emphasis is justified to maintain public confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor leaders and grassroots rumblings (listening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders live 'with their ears to the ground' for rumblings of public sentiment; counsel must monitor these signals to time and shape messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously surveil opinion leaders, clergy, critics, and public sentiment to avoid tactless delivery and to intensify receptive moments rather than attempt manufacture of sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use coalition-building and shared public service appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigns that are presented as public service (not mere advocacy) can enlist cooperation from other institutions and media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame initiatives as serving a public good (e.g., campaigns against coal monopoly, anti-theater ticket speculator law) to attract partners and broaden reach.
